content: At least one billion cases of vision impairment worldwide could have been prevented or remain undiagnosed. By 2030, this number is projected to reach one billion. The situation may worsen due to increasing life expectancy and lifestyle changes. Approximately 90% of individuals with vision loss live in lowand middle-income countries. Currently, five million people require surgery for trachomatous trichiasis. The World Health Organization (WHO) aims to eliminate trachoma as a public health issue by 2030 using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, and Environmental improvement) and WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) initiatives. Nearly 30% of the global population with blindness or vision impairment resides in the WHO South-East Asia Region. In adults, common causes of vision impairment include uncorrected refractive errors, cataracts, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, corneal scarring, and trachoma. In children, the leading causes are uncorrected refractive errors, cataracts, retinopathy of prematurity, congenital ocular anomalies, corneal scarring, and cerebral visual impairment. The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) has categorized 11 countries in the WHO South-East Asia Region into three subregions: South-East Asia (Indonesia, Maldives, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Timor-Leste), South Asia (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal), and East Asia (Democratic People’s Republic of Korea). This region bears a significant burden of eye diseases. Globally, trachoma remains a public health problem in 43 countries. However, as of March 2022, 14 countries have achieved elimination goals. Within the South-East Asia Region, Myanmar (2020) and Nepal (2018) have been verified for trachoma elimination in recent years. Addressing eye health is critical for overall health, poverty reduction, improved education, and socio-economic growth. Universal eye health care contributes to achieving multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is essential for universal health coverage (UHC). Member states have committed to universal eye health through various discussions, decisions, and resolutions. Currently, one billion people with vision impairment lack access to necessary eye care services. The WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia mandated the development of a regional action plan for integrated, people-centered eye care (IPEC) in 2021. This plan aligns with the 2030 global targets for effective cataract surgery coverage and refractive error coverage, endorsed by the World Health Assembly. The 2019 World Report on Vision emphasizes integrating eye health into UHC efforts and implementing IPEC within reoriented health systems focused on primary health care. IPEC ensures a continuum of care, addressing the full spectrum of eye conditions through promotion, prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation. It emphasizes coordination across care levels and recognizes individuals as active participants in their care throughout their lives. The integration of eye care services can be achieved through multidisciplinary teams of health and social workers engaged with communities. Opportunities exist to incorporate eye care into various levels of health care delivery, from primary to tertiary care, and through outreach programs. The WHO proposes global eye care targets, including a 40-percentage-point increase in effective refractive error coverage and a 30-percentage-point increase in effective cataract surgery coverage by 2030. Additionally, regional targets include ensuring at least 80% of people with diabetes are regularly screened for retinopathy and treated for sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, and eliminating trachoma in the region by 2025. Guiding principles for the action plan include universality, member state leadership, evidence-based actions, people-centeredness, and leveraging technology. Strategies focus on engaging and empowering communities, reorienting care models to prioritize primary and community-based services, and ensuring functional referral linkages. Strategic actions include improving public awareness, integrating eye disease screening into health programs, promoting school-based eye health initiatives, and developing programs for underserved populations. Technology, such as telemedicine, can enhance access and coverage of eye care services, particularly in remote areas.
